newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine '96 trade deficit at record high.
newsitem.headline: Philippine '96 trade deficit at record high.

text.p: The Philippine government said on Friday its merchandise trade deficit climbed to a record high of $11.786 billion in 1996 from the year-ago $9.091 billion, but economists described the trade gap as lower than expected.

The National Statistics Office (NSO) said in a statement that Philippine import bills grew by 21.8 percent to $32.329 billion in 1996 from the previous $26.538 billion while receipts from exports improved by 17.7 percent to $20.543 billion from $17.447 billion.
"The figures were better. We were expecting a trade deficit of between $12.2 billion and $12.5 billion in 1996," economist Alvin Ang of All Asia Capital and Trust Corp told Reuters.
Gina Dipaling, an analyst at Philippine Asia Equity Securities Phils Inc, also said the figure was lower than her earlier forecast of $12.6 billion.
Analysts attributed the slightly lower trade deficit numbers compared with earlier forecasts to lower imports in December, 1996.
The NSO said the merchandise trade deficit in December 1996 reached $835 million compared to $950 million in December 1995.
Export revenues in the last month of 1996 also grew by 16.2 percent while import bills inched up only by 5.7 percent, it added.
In November 1996, exports grew by 30 percent while imports rose 12.3 percent.
Analysts said they expect the country's trade deficit to widen further this year due to more capital equipment imports.

"This is necessary to sustain the rising momentum of a growing economy. Besides, materials used in the assembly of electronics are mostly sourced abroad because chip manufacturers are only starting to sprout in the country," said Noel Reyes, vice president at Anscor Hagedorn Securities. Electronics comprises almost half of the country's exports.
Jonas Ferrer, the research director of Pryce Securities, said he expected the trade deficit this year to rise to $14 billion while Asia Equity's Dipaling said she expected it to hit $15 billion.
All Asia's Ang also forecast a 1997 deficit of $14 billion, while Asian Bank forecast a figure between $15 billion and $17 billion.

Analysts say they see import bills rising further due to the massive expansion programme of the country's 12 telephone operators, aicraft acquisition by flag carrier Philippine Airlines Inc (PAL) and other infrastructure expenditure by both the government and private sector.
"Imports of capital equipment and raw materials are necessary for a growing economy. What we should ask is can the Philippines afford it?", Reyes said.
Reyes said the Philippines can afford to finance its capital expenditures because of the country's high level of foreign reserves.
The presidential palace said on Saturday that Philippine gross international reserves reached $11.76 billion as of January 27 this year, up from $11.74 billion at the end of December.
